Text:
Patient assessment is divided into five main parts, in order:

1. {{c1::Scene size-up}}

2. {{c1::Primary assessment}}

3. {{c1::History taking}}

4. {{c1::Secondary assessment}}

5. {{c1::Reassessment}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the order may vary with the patient's condition and the environment — some steps may be reordered after scene size-up to prioritize care.

Cue: the same five parts are used for both medical and trauma patients.

Text: A {{c1::symptom}} is a {{c2::subjective}} condition — one the patient {{c2::feels and tells you about}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: a sign is objective — you can observe or measure it.

Text:
While assessing a man hurt in a low-speed car crash:

He says his neck hurts — a {{c1::symptom::sign or symptom}}

You see a swollen, deformed forearm — a {{c1::sign::sign or symptom}}
Back Extra:
Why: a symptom is felt and reported by the patient (subjective); a sign is something you observe or measure (objective).

Cue: rarely does one sign or symptom reveal the problem — the combination directs your care.

Text: A {{c1::sign}} is an {{c2::objective}} condition — one {{c2::you can observe or measure}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: a symptom is subjective — only the patient can feel it, and must tell you about it.

Text: During scene size-up, watch the ground for uneven or unstable surfaces, water, mud, and ice {{c1::before you step out of the response vehicle::when}}.
Back Extra: Why: you carry gear and a stretcher in, and bring out a loaded stretcher plus equipment — footing that was compromised going in is even harder coming out.

Text: You notice an unsecured hammer on the nightstand beside your patient. Position yourself {{c1::between the patient and the hammer::where}}.
Back Extra:
Why: your body blocks the patient's possible access to an object that could become a weapon.

Cue: weapons are not just knives and guns — household items such as a screwdriver or hammer count.

Pitfall: request law enforcement as soon as you think a scene may turn violent.

Text: Traumatic injuries are the result of {{c1::physical forces}} applied to the {{c1::outside}} of the body.
Back Extra:
Ex: an object striking the body, or the body striking an object.

Distinguish: a medical problem needs no outside force — for those patients you determine the nature of illness (NOI) rather than an MOI.

Text: The {{c1::mechanism of injury (MOI)::term}} describes how a trauma occurred: the {{c2::type or amount}} of force, {{c2::how long}} it was applied, and {{c2::where}} it was applied to the body.
Back Extra:
Why: the MOI is a guide that helps you focus your assessment.

Cue: fragile parts (brain, spinal cord, eyes) are injured by even small forces; bones and certain organs can absorb small forces.

Text:
Classify the assessment focus for each call:

A roofer who fell from a ladder — evaluate the {{c1::mechanism of injury (MOI)::MOI or NOI}}

A woman with sudden, crushing chest pain — evaluate the {{c1::nature of illness (NOI)::MOI or NOI}}
Back Extra:
Why: an outside physical force means trauma, so you size up the MOI; an illness with no outside force means a medical call, so you determine the NOI.

Cue: both the MOI and the NOI direct your assessment and your care.

Text: For a medical patient (no injuring outside force), you determine the general type of problem, or the {{c1::nature of illness (NOI)::term}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: a patient who says he feels as if he cannot get enough air — his NOI is difficulty breathing.

Cue: the NOI is often best described by the patient's chief complaint, and like the MOI it directs both your assessment and your care.

Text: Standard precautions treat even {{c2::dried}} blood and body fluids as potentially infectious, because some diseases, such as hepatitis, can live for {{c1::days::how long}} outside the body.
Back Extra:
Why: standard precautions assume all blood, body fluids, nonintact skin, and mucous membranes may pose a substantial risk of infection.

Cue: take standard precautions before actual patient contact — often before you even step out of the response vehicle.

Text: At a minimum, {{c1::gloves}} and {{c1::eye protection}} must be in place before any patient contact.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: handwashing, a mask, and a gown may be added by local protocol or the situation — gloves and eye protection are the floor for every contact.

Pitfall: after patient contact your gloves may be contaminated — do not handle EMS equipment with the same gloves.

Text: The {{c1::incident command system (ICS)::structure}} is a {{c2::flexible}} system implemented to manage {{c2::a variety of emergency scenes}}, used when you have multiple patients.
Back Extra:
Cue: with multiple patients — establish command, identify the number of patients, then begin triage.

Why: an accurate patient count determines your need for additional resources (firefighters, rescue, hazmat, more ambulances).

Text: At a multiple-patient incident, responders work in groups organized by {{c1::function or assigned area::2 criteria}}, with each group leader reporting to the {{c2::incident commander::role}}.
Back Extra: Meaning: the incident commander is the person in charge of the whole incident.

Text: As the first part of your primary assessment, the {{c1::general impression::assessment step}} focuses on {{c2::rapid identification of potentially life-threatening problems}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the general impression determines the priority of care.

Cue: formed as you approach — noting the patient's age, sex, race, level of distress, and overall appearance.

Text:
Uncontrolled external bleeding is suggested by a large amount of blood that:

is {{c1::squirting or gushing}}

has {{c1::soaked through clothing}}

is {{c1::pooling under the patient}}

Life-threatening external bleeding is controlled {{c2::before::before or after}} the assessment proceeds.
Back Extra:
Cue: the determination is somewhat subjective — a judgment call, not an exact measurement.

Why: uncontrolled external bleeding takes priority over the other assessments.

Text: Forming your general impression of a man cut by a chainsaw, you see a large amount of blood flowing from his thigh and pooling beneath him. What is your first action? {{c1::Control the bleeding::next step}}
Back Extra: Why: life-threatening external bleeding is controlled before the assessment proceeds — it takes priority over the other assessments.

Text:
The AVPU scale grades a patient's gross level of consciousness by responsiveness, at one of four levels:

{{c1::Awake and alert::A}}

{{c1::Responsive to verbal stimuli::V}}

{{c1::Responsive to pain::P}}

{{c1::Unresponsive::U}}
Back Extra:
Cue: graded by response to external stimuli — verbal stimuli (sound) and painful stimuli (such as pinching the trapezius muscle on top of the shoulder).

Why: in the primary assessment you need to ascertain only the gross LOC.
verified_by: agent; first_letter_hint cleared: AVPU is a spelled mnemonic, bold in the stem, letters printed beside each level on p945/946/948 - rule 18 license (only A/U literally match first letters; V/P key the discriminating word)

Text: On the AVPU scale, an awake and alert patient differs from one merely responsive to verbal stimuli in that the alert patient's eyes open {{c1::spontaneously, as you approach::eye-opening trigger}} — not only when spoken to.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the full alert picture — aware of and responsive to the environment, follows commands, and the eyes visually track people and objects.

Ex: a meaningful response to verbal stimuli can be as little as moaning, speaking, or moving.

Text: A woman's eyes stay closed when you ask her name in a normal voice, but she groans and stirs when you shout. On the AVPU scale she is graded {{c1::responsive to (loud) verbal stimuli::V or P}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: needing a loud voice is still a verbal response — responsive to pain requires no response to any voice, with a response only to a painful stimulus.

Cue: chart exactly how she responded — 'responds to loud verbal stimuli.'

Text: When a patient who has not responded to verbal stimuli is given a painful stimulus, {{c1::moving or crying out::response}} grades the patient P (responsive to pain), while {{c1::staying flaccid, with no movement or sound::response}} grades the patient U (unresponsive).
Back Extra:
Pitfall: some painful-stimulus methods may not give an accurate result if a spinal cord injury is present.

Cue: record the type and location of the stimulus and how the patient responded.

Text: Unresponsive patients usually have no {{c1::cough or gag}} reflex and so lack the ability to {{c1::protect their airway}}.
Back Extra: Pitfall: if you are in doubt about whether a patient is truly unresponsive, assume the worst and treat appropriately.

Text: You find a man who does not respond to your voice or to a firm ear-lobe pinch. Assume he cannot {{c1::protect his airway::ability lost}}.
Back Extra: Mechanism: unresponsiveness usually means no cough or gag reflex — nothing protects the airway.

Text:
A patient does not respond to verbal stimuli, so you test the response to pain. Gently but firmly pinch or press at the three sites where the technique works best, or use one further pressure technique:

{{c1::sternum::site}}

{{c1::posterior edge of the mandible (lower jaw)::site}}

{{c1::trapezius area (the muscle above the collar bone)::site}}

{{c1::upward pressure along the ridge of the orbital rim, on the underside of the eyebrow::technique}}
Back Extra:
Why: the point is not to cause as much pain as possible, but to see whether the patient responds to or withdraws from the sensation.

Pitfall: with the orbital-rim technique, apply no pressure to the eyeball.

Text: Once the LOC is graded, for a patient who is {{c3::alert or responsive to verbal stimuli::which AVPU grades}} you next evaluate {{c1::orientation::what you evaluate}}, which tests mental status by checking the patient's {{c2::memory and thinking ability}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: the AVPU grade measures responsiveness to stimuli; orientation measures memory and thinking.

Text:
The most common orientation test checks the patient's ability to remember four things:

{{c1::Person — his or her own name}}

{{c1::Place — the current location}}

{{c1::Time — the current year, month, and day of the week}}

{{c1::Event — what happened (the MOI or NOI)}}
Back Extra:
Why: the questions were not selected at random — it is paramount to assess all four.

Cue: all four intact = 'alert and fully oriented,' or 'alert and oriented × 4.'

Text: A woman gives her name and location but cannot tell you the year or what happened, and her family says she is normally sharp. Her mental status is {{c1::altered::altered or normal}}.
Back Extra:
Why: she is oriented only to person and place — any deviation from alert-and-oriented to person, place, time, and event, or from her own baseline, is an altered mental status.

Distinguish: a patient whose everyday baseline is not fully oriented (for example, from developmental delay) is judged against that baseline instead.

Text:
The four orientation questions sample three tiers of memory:

Long-term memory — {{c1::person and place}}

Intermediate memory — {{c1::place, and time when asking the year or month}}

Short-term memory — {{c1::time when asking the approximate day of the week, and the event}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: place counts toward long-term AND intermediate memory; time counts toward intermediate (year/month) AND short-term (day of the week).

Cue: person is the oldest memory (your own name); the event is the newest (what just happened).
verified_by: agent; undercount cleared: 'four' counts the orientation questions (visible anchor); the clozed list is the three tiers, 3/3 verified vs p950 render, and all four questions appear inside the tier answers

Text: Any deviation from alert and oriented to person, place, time, and event — or from the patient's own {{c2::normal baseline}} — is considered {{c1::an altered mental status::finding}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: ongoing illness, history of stroke, traumatic brain injury, developmental delay, or Alzheimer disease can give a patient a baseline of not being fully alert and oriented.

Cue: determine the patient's normal mental status whenever possible.

Text:
Three findings (any one alone is enough) indicate spinal immobilization after either blunt or penetrating trauma:

{{c1::pain or tenderness on palpation of the neck or spine}}

{{c1::patient report of pain in the neck or back}}

{{c1::paralysis or a neurologic complaint (numbness, tingling, partial paralysis of the legs or arms)}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: tenderness is what you find on palpation; reported pain is what the patient tells you — either one counts.

Roster: blunt OR penetrating trauma — pain/tenderness on palpation of the neck or spine, patient report of neck or back pain, paralysis or neurologic complaint. Blunt trauma only — altered mental status, intoxication, difficulty or inability to communicate. By itself — distracting injury.

Text:
Three findings (any one alone is enough) indicate spinal immobilization only when the trauma is blunt:

{{c1::altered mental status}}

{{c1::intoxication (alcohol or drugs)}}

{{c1::difficulty or inability to communicate}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: pain/tenderness and neurologic findings count after blunt OR penetrating trauma; altered mental status, intoxication, and communication difficulty count only after blunt.

Roster: blunt OR penetrating trauma — pain/tenderness on palpation of the neck or spine, patient report of neck or back pain, paralysis or neurologic complaint. Blunt trauma only — altered mental status, intoxication, difficulty or inability to communicate. By itself — distracting injury.

Text: {{c1::A distracting injury::injury category}} is by itself an indication for spinal immobilization, even when the patient has no other findings.
Back Extra:
Meaning: any injury that pulls the patient's attention away from other injuries he or she may have — even severe ones.

Why: severe pain from one injury can keep the patient from noticing neck or back pain from an unstable fracture.

Roster: blunt OR penetrating trauma — pain/tenderness on palpation of the neck or spine, patient report of neck or back pain, paralysis or neurologic complaint. Blunt trauma only — altered mental status, intoxication, difficulty or inability to communicate. By itself — distracting injury.

Text: A driver who smells of alcohol and admits drinking heavily is pulled from his crashed car, alert and fully oriented. He denies neck or back pain, with no tenderness and no neurologic complaint. Spinal immobilization {{c1::is::is / is not}} indicated.
Back Extra:
Why: with blunt trauma, intoxication alone is a sufficient indication — a clean, fully oriented exam does not remove it.

Distinguish: intoxication, altered mental status, and communication difficulty are indications only with BLUNT trauma; pain/tenderness and neurologic findings apply to blunt or penetrating trauma.

Text: Because a painful fracture can mask spine pain, all patients with a {{c1::long bone::fracture type}} fracture and a {{c1::significant::MOI qualifier}} MOI warrant spinal immobilization.
Back Extra:
Why: the fracture acts as a distracting injury, preventing the patient from reliably identifying neck or back pain from an unstable fracture.

Cue: the two keys are the fracture type (long bone) and the MOI (significant) — both must be present.

Text: A motorcyclist thrown at highway speed has an obviously deformed, painful femur but insists his neck and back feel fine. Beyond caring for the leg, you should still {{c1::apply spinal immobilization::precaution}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the femur is a distracting injury — its pain can mask neck or back pain from an unstable spine fracture.

Cue: long bone fracture plus significant MOI warrants spinal immobilization, whatever the patient reports.

Text: To prevent {{c2::death or permanent disability::two outcomes}}, ensure your patient's airway remains {{c1::open (patent)::airway state}} and adequate.
Back Extra:
Cue: a patient of any age who is talking or crying has an open airway.

Pitfall: a conscious patient who cannot speak or cry most likely has a severe airway obstruction — stop the assessment process and work to clear the airway.

Text:
Opening an unresponsive patient's airway:

Any potential for trauma → the {{c1::jaw-thrust}} maneuver

If the {{c1::jaw-thrust}} fails to yield a patent airway, or trauma is ruled out → the {{c1::head tilt-chin lift}} maneuver
Back Extra:
Pitfall: in an unconscious patient the tongue often relaxes and falls to the back of the throat — address it first by positioning the airway, then with an oral or nasal airway.

Cue: dentures, blood clots, vomitus, mucus, and food can also obstruct, and are cleared manually or with suction.

Text: You find an unresponsive man crumpled at the base of a ladder. Which maneuver do you use first to open his airway? {{c1::The jaw-thrust maneuver}}
Back Extra:
Why: unresponsive patients may have experienced a traumatic event — any potential for trauma means jaw-thrust first.

Cue: switch to the head tilt-chin lift only if the jaw-thrust fails to give a patent airway, or trauma is confidently excluded.

Text:
In an unconscious patient, the signs of airway obstruction are:

{{c1::Obvious trauma, blood, or other obstruction}}

{{c1::Noisy breathing (snoring, bubbling, gurgling, crowing, stridor, or other abnormal sounds)}}

{{c1::Extremely shallow or absent breathing}}
Back Extra:
Cue: normal breathing is quiet — any added sound is obstruction until proven otherwise.

Why: with any of these present the airway is inadequate — open it (jaw-thrust if trauma is possible, otherwise head tilt-chin lift), suction, and place an airway adjunct as needed; an unmanaged airway starves the body of oxygen.

Text: A patient who is {{c2::breathing without assistance}} is said to have {{c1::spontaneous respirations::term}}.
Back Extra: Cue: three questions then judge those breaths — Is the patient breathing? Is the breathing adequate? Is the patient hypoxic?

Text:
In the primary assessment, the breathing findings decide the intervention:

Not breathing, or breathing too slow or too shallow → {{c1::provide positive-pressure ventilations::action}}

Breathing adequately but still hypoxic → {{c1::administer oxygen::action}}
Back Extra:
Cue: consider positive-pressure ventilations with an airway adjunct when respirations exceed 28 breaths/min with signs of distress, are fewer than 8 breaths/min, or are too shallow for adequate air exchange — air exchange, not the number of breaths, is the critical issue.

Pitfall: oxygen alone does nothing for a patient who is not moving air — inadequate breathing needs ventilation, not just supplemental O2.
verified_by: agent — 28 and 8 breaths/min verified verbatim on the p955 render (Back Extra cue); editor re-verified both digits on p955

Text: A man's breathing is rapid but so shallow his chest barely moves; his neck muscles strain and the skin pulls in between his ribs with each breath. Beyond oxygen, what should you consider? {{c1::Positive-pressure ventilations (with an airway adjunct)::intervention}}
Back Extra:
Cue: retractions plus accessory-muscle use = inadequate breathing; too shallow to exchange air = ventilate.

Pitfall: a fast rate can look like the effort is working — air exchange, not the number of breaths, is the critical issue.

Text: A calm woman is breathing at a normal rate with full, easy chest rise, but her oxygen saturation reads 90%. What do you do? {{c1::Administer oxygen::PPV or oxygen}}
Back Extra:
Why: her breathing is adequate, so she needs oxygenation, not ventilation — the goal is a saturation above 94%.

Distinguish: positive-pressure ventilations are reserved for absent, too-slow, or too-shallow breathing.
verified_by: agent — scenario built on the verified >94% goal from the p955 render; 90% is a below-goal exemplar value; editor re-verified the goal on p955

Text: For most patients, the goal for oxygenation is an oxygen saturation of greater than {{c1::94}}%.
Back Extra:
Cue: breathing adequately but sitting below the goal = hypoxic — administer oxygen.

Pitfall: a good saturation number never overrides inadequate breathing — too-slow or too-shallow breathing still needs positive-pressure ventilations.
verified_by: agent — 94% verified verbatim on the p955 render; editor re-verified 'greater than 94%' on p955

Text: {{c1::Shallow::depth descriptor}} respirations show {{c2::little movement of the chest wall}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: deep respirations cause a significant rise and fall of the chest — document either extreme.

Why: little chest movement = reduced tidal volume and poor chest excursion — each breath moves too little air, so even a normal rate can fail to provide adequate air exchange.

Text: {{c1::Retractions::sign}} are {{c2::indentations above the clavicles and between the ribs}} — like accessory-muscle use, a sign of inadequate breathing.
Back Extra:
Cue: watch how much effort breathing requires — retractions and accessory-muscle use mean the body is recruiting extra help to move air.

Distinguish: in pediatric patients the parallel signs are nasal flaring and seesaw breathing.

Text:
The accessory muscles of respiration are three groups:

{{c1::the neck muscles (sternocleidomastoid)}}

{{c1::the chest pectoralis major muscles}}

{{c1::the abdominal muscles}}
Back Extra: Cue: normal breathing is an effortless process — visible use of these groups is a sign of inadequate breathing, as are retractions.
verified_by: agent — closed 3-group list verified on the p955 render; editor re-verified: exactly neck (SCM), chest pectoralis major, abdominal

Text: In pediatric patients, {{c1::nasal flaring}} and {{c1::seesaw breathing}} indicate inadequate breathing.
Back Extra: Distinguish: retractions and accessory-muscle use flag inadequate breathing in general — flaring and seesaw breathing are the pediatric-specific tells.

Text: A patient sitting upright with the head and chin thrust slightly forward is in the {{c1::sniffing::posture}} position, seen most commonly in {{c2::children::age group}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the tripod position — sitting, leaning forward on outstretched arms — is the other airflow-maximizing posture, and demands significant conscious effort to breathe.

Why: patients in marked difficulty instinctively assume the posture that makes breathing easier.

Cue: the name is literal — the patient appears to be sniffing the air.

Text: {{c1::Labored::descriptor}} breathing is breathing with {{c2::visible effort}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: early tells are the patient's position, concentration on breathing, and increased effort and depth of each breath; as it worsens, chest and neck accessory muscles engage and the patient may grunt with each breath.

Ex: in infants and small children it commonly brings nasal flaring, supraclavicular and intercostal retractions, and sometimes gasping.

Text: Infants and small children may sustain labored breathing for a long period, but then often become {{c1::exhausted}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a small child still working hard to breathe is on a clock — the crash comes when the effort runs out.

Why: once exhausted, they no longer have the strength to maintain the energy needed to breathe.

Cue: grunting, gasping, nasal flaring, and supraclavicular/intercostal retractions mark labored breathing in infants and small children.

Text: In infants and small children, cardiac arrest is generally caused by {{c1::respiratory arrest}}.
Back Extra:
Pathway: respiratory distress → respiratory failure → (uncorrected) respiratory arrest → cardiac arrest.

Why: breathing failure comes first in children — aggressive airway and ventilation care is what prevents the cardiac arrest.

Text:
As respiratory distress deteriorates into respiratory failure, the patient's whole drive winds down:

Agitation, anxiety, restlessness become {{c1::lethargy, difficult to rouse}}

Mild tachycardia becomes {{c1::bradycardia}}

Nasal flaring, seesaw breathing, head bobbing give way to {{c1::diminished muscle tone}}
Back Extra:
Why: distress means working harder to breathe (effort and rate up); failure means the work is no longer oxygenating the blood — the winding-down child is running out, not settling down.

Pitfall: an agitated child who seems to be "calming" may actually be slipping into failure — reassess, don't relax.

Roster: failure signs — lethargy/difficult to rouse · tachypnea with periods of bradypnea or agonal respirations · inadequate chest rise/poor excursion · inadequate respiratory rate or effort · bradycardia · diminished muscle tone

Text:
As respiratory distress deteriorates into respiratory failure, the breathing itself gives out:

Stridor and wheezing become {{c1::tachypnea with periods of bradypnea, or agonal respirations}}

Tachypnea becomes {{c1::an inadequate respiratory rate or effort}}

Accessory-muscle use with intercostal retractions and neck-muscle use becomes {{c1::inadequate chest rise / poor excursion}}
Back Extra:
Why: respiratory failure means the blood is inadequately oxygenated or ventilation cannot meet the body's oxygen demands — and uncorrected, its ultimate result is respiratory arrest.

Roster: failure signs — lethargy/difficult to rouse · tachypnea with periods of bradypnea or agonal respirations · inadequate chest rise/poor excursion · inadequate respiratory rate or effort · bradycardia · diminished muscle tone

Text: Although often called a heartbeat, the {{c1::pulse}} is really {{c2::the pressure wave}} sent through the arteries by each heartbeat.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a heartbeat is the ventricular contraction itself, forcefully ejecting blood into the arteries; the pulse is the traveling wave that surge creates.

Cue: feel the pulse at a pulse point, where a major artery lies near the surface and can be pressed gently against a bone or solid organ.

Text:
Where you palpate the pulse depends on age and responsiveness:

Responsive and older than 1 year → {{c1::radial (at the wrist)}}

Unresponsive and older than 1 year → {{c1::carotid (at the neck)}}

Younger than 1 year → {{c1::brachial (inside of the upper arm)}}
Back Extra:
Why: in infants, the radial and carotid pulses are simply difficult to locate, so the brachial is the site regardless of responsiveness.

Pitfall: never palpate any pulse with your thumb; you may mistake its own strong pulsing for the patient's.

Text: A mother hands you her limp 7-month-old, who does not respond to your voice or touch. Which pulse do you palpate? {{c1::Brachial}}
Back Extra:
Why: under 1 year the radial and carotid pulses are difficult to locate, so the brachial is the site even though she is unresponsive.

Pitfall: "unresponsive → carotid" applies only to patients older than 1 year.

Text: With an infant lying supine, you can reach the brachial pulse by {{c1::elevating the arm over the infant's head::arm maneuver}}.
Back Extra: Cue: infant arms are chubby, so press adjacent fingertips firmly along the brachial artery, which runs parallel to the long axis of the upper arm.

Text:
Your patient is unresponsive:

No palpable carotid pulse → begin {{c1::CPR}}

Pulse present but not breathing → provide {{c1::ventilations}}
Back Extra: Distinguish: the choice applies only to unresponsive patients — never begin CPR or use an AED on a responsive one.

Text: You find a 58-year-old man collapsed at a gym. He does not respond to painful stimulus, and you cannot palpate a carotid pulse. What do you do first? {{c1::Begin CPR}}
Back Extra:
Why: unresponsive + no palpable carotid pulse = begin CPR; when the AED arrives, turn it on and follow its voice prompts.

Distinguish: had he been responsive, no CPR and no AED — an unfelt pulse in a responsive patient is not cardiac arrest.
verified_by: agent; open_set_absolute cleared: 'cannot' is a clinical finding inside the vignette stem, not a prohibition rule — the unresponsive + pulseless state forces exactly one action (card-rules #16's own fix)

Text: If an AED is available for your unresponsive, pulseless patient, turn it on and follow its {{c1::voice prompts}}, consistent with your {{c1::local protocol}}.
Back Extra: Why: an AED is indicated only for patients already assessed to be unresponsive and pulseless — the pulse check comes before the machine.

Text: An adult who has a pulse but is not breathing gets ventilations at a rate of {{c1::10 to 12}} breaths/min.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: rescue ventilations are for a patient who still HAS a pulse — a pulseless patient gets CPR and the AED instead.

Roster: rescue-ventilation rates — adult 10 to 12; infant or child 12 to 20 breaths/min.

Text: An infant or child who has a pulse but is not breathing gets ventilations at a rate of {{c1::12 to 20}} breaths/min.
Back Extra:
Cue: infants and children share a single range — there is no separate infant band for rescue ventilations.

Roster: rescue-ventilation rates — adult 10 to 12; infant or child 12 to 20 breaths/min.

Text: While ventilating a patient who has a pulse but is not breathing, recheck the pulse every {{c1::2}} minutes to evaluate the effectiveness of your ventilations.
Back Extra: Why: a lost pulse is the failure signal — the moment the patient becomes pulseless, start CPR and apply the AED.

Text: You must never begin CPR or use an AED on a {{c1::responsive::responsive/unresponsive}} patient — apparent pulselessness in that patient is not cardiac arrest.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: an AED is indicated only for patients assessed to be unresponsive AND pulseless — the exact opposite state.

Pitfall: a hard-to-feel pulse alone does not license CPR; responsiveness overrules your fingers.

Text: Skin with inadequate blood flow turns {{c1::pale::color}} and {{c1::cool::temperature}} — a warning of possible hypoperfusion of the {{c2::brain, lungs, heart, and kidneys::4 organs}}. In most situations, hypoperfusion is caused by {{c3::shock::cause}}.
Back Extra:
Why: normally perfused skin holds its usual color, temperature, and moisture, which is why skin is one of the most accessible windows on circulation.

Pitfall: the degree and duration of hypoperfusion determine whether the patient sustains permanent injury.

Text: You reach a motorcyclist lying beside his bike; his skin looks pale, gray, and waxy, and feels cool through your gloves. Skin findings like his should make you suspect {{c1::hypoperfusion (shock)::underlying problem}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: pale, white, ashen, or gray skin with a waxy, translucent look is the face of poor peripheral circulation — and in most situations hypoperfusion is caused by shock.

Pitfall: abnormally cold or frozen skin can take on the same pale, waxy look.

Text: {{c1::The blood circulating through vessels near the surface}} and {{c1::the amount and type of pigment}} are the two factors that determine a patient's skin color.
Back Extra: Why: pigment sets the baseline; the circulating blood is the part that changes with perfusion and oxygenation — so skin color reads the circulation.

Text: The {{c1::conjunctiva::eye structure}} is the {{c2::membrane lining the eyelids and eye surface}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: in deeply pigmented skin, color changes may show only at low-pigment sites — nail beds, lips, mouth mucosa, the underside of the arm and palm, and the conjunctiva; in infants and children, also check palms and soles.

Distinguish: the sclera is the white wall of the eye itself; the conjunctiva is the thin membrane over it and inside the lids.

Text: In a patient with insufficient air exchange, the lips, mucous membranes, and nail beds turn blue or gray because {{c2::the blood is not properly saturated with oxygen}} — a color change called {{c1::cyanosis::condition}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: blue shows where vessels run near the surface — lips, mucous membranes, nail beds, and the skin directly over blood vessels.

Distinguish: pale, ashen, waxy skin means too little blood flow; blue-gray means blood is flowing but poorly oxygenated.

Text: {{c1::High blood pressure::cardiovascular cause}} may make the skin abnormally flushed and red.
Back Extra:
Ex: significant fever, heatstroke, sunburn, and mild thermal burns also redden the skin — conditions in which the body cannot properly dissipate heat.

Distinguish: red = pressure or heat; blue-gray = low oxygen; pale = low flow.

Text: Yellow skin and sclera — a color change called {{c2::jaundice::condition}} — suggest {{c1::liver::organ}} disease or dysfunction.
Back Extra: Distinguish: pallor points to poor blood flow and cyanosis to poor oxygenation — jaundice instead reflects chronic illness (the liver).

Text: The {{c1::sclera::eye part}} is the {{c2::normally white portion of the eye}}, and it may show color changes {{c3::before::before or after}} the skin does.
Back Extra:
Cue: in jaundice both the skin and sclera turn yellow — and the eye often flags it first.

Distinguish: the conjunctiva is the delicate membrane lining the eyelids and covering the eye's exposed surface — a separate structure from the white sclera behind it.

Text: The sclera is {{c1::the white outer coat of the eye}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Liver disease or dysfunction may cause jaundice, resulting in the patient's skin and sclera turning yellow."

Cue: the sclera can show a color change (jaundice yellowing) even before the skin does.

Parts: scler- (hard) — the eye's tough shell; same root as sclerosis.

Formal: "the tough, fibrous, white portion of the eye that protects the more delicate inner structures."

Text: Normal skin feels warm to the touch. Normal body temperature is {{c1::98.6°F (37°C)}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: the abnormal skin temperatures are hot, cool, cold, and clammy (moist).

Text:
The skin feels cool in three situations:

{{c1::early shock}}

{{c1::mild hypothermia}}

{{c1::inadequate perfusion}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: cold skin goes deeper — profound shock, hypothermia, or frostbite; hot skin means significant fever, sunburn, or hyperthermia.

Cue: with poor perfusion the body pulls blood from the skin's surface to the core — cool, pale, clammy skin in the primary assessment is a strong indication of hypoperfusion and shock.

Text: In the {{c1::early::early or late}} stages of shock, the skin becomes {{c2::slightly moist::moisture finding}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: shock can also bathe the skin in sweat (wet, diaphoretic) — slight moisture is specifically the early-stage finding.

Cue: consider moisture together with color and temperature — the three are related signs and travel as one picture.

Text:
Describing skin moisture in your report:

only a slight film of sweat, not soaked → {{c1::clammy, damp, or moist::3 terms}}

bathed in sweat → {{c1::wet or diaphoretic::2 terms}}
Back Extra:
Cue: both strenuous exercise and shock can leave a patient bathed in sweat.

Pitfall: dry skin is the normal state; skin that is moist or wet from sweat suggests a problem — and slight moisture can already mean early shock.

Text: A 60-year-old has just finished a road race; sweat has soaked through his shirt and drips from his chin. You record his skin moisture as {{c1::wet (diaphoretic)::moisture term}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: a light film of moisture with a dry shirt would be recorded as clammy (damp, moist) instead.

Text: Diaphoresis is {{c1::profuse, drenching sweating}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "When the skin is bathed in sweat, such as after strenuous exercise or when the patient is in shock, the skin is described as wet or diaphoretic."

Parts: dia- (through) + phor- (carry) — sweat carried out through the skin.

Distinguish: clammy = only slightly moist skin; diaphoretic = skin bathed in sweat.

Formal: "diaphoretic: characterized by light or profuse sweating."

Text:
When recording or reporting your skin assessment, describe the findings in this order:

1. {{c1::color}}

2. {{c1::temperature}}

3. {{c1::moisture}}
Back Extra:
Ex: "Skin: pale, cool, and clammy."

Why: color, temperature, and moisture are often related signs, so consider them together and report them as one ordered picture.

Text: To test capillary refill, gently compress the patient's fingertip with your {{c1::thumb}} on the fingernail and your {{c1::fingers}} on the underside of the finger, until the nail bed {{c2::blanches (turns white)::color change}}.
Back Extra: Why: compressing forces blood out of the nail-bed capillaries; after release, the time back to normal pink is the capillaries refilling — the thing you are counting.

Text: A 4-year-old fell from a playground slide. You compress her nail bed, release, and count "one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand, three-one-thousand" before pink returns. Her refill time is {{c1::too slow::normal or too slow}}, so you should {{c1::suspect poor peripheral circulation::conclusion}}.
Back Extra:
Why: normal capillary refill is 2 seconds or less — three seconds is too slow.

Distinguish: an injured extremity can have locally compromised circulation, so slow refill in one limb may mean local hypoperfusion rather than hypoperfusion of the whole body.
verified_by: agent; editor cleared grounding warning: 'too slow' is the vignette's applied verdict of the verified >2 s threshold (p968), a paraphrase not an addition

Text:
To assess capillary refill in {{c2::newborns and young infants::age group}}, press on one of three sites:

{{c1::the forehead}}

{{c1::the chin}}

{{c1::the sternum}}
Back Extra: Distinguish: the standard site is the fingertip nail bed, compressed until it blanches — the three body sites replace it in the very young.

Text: With adequate perfusion, a blanched nail bed returns to its normal pink within {{c1::2 seconds}}. Slower refill — or a nail bed that stays blanched — means you should suspect {{c2::poor peripheral circulation::conclusion}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: normal refill takes about the time it takes to say "capillary refill" at a normal rate of speech.

Ex: report and document a normal result as CRT of 2 seconds or less.

Text: Serious bleeding from a large vein is characterized by a {{c1::steady::steady or spurting}} flow of blood, whereas bleeding from an artery is characterized by a {{c1::spurting::steady or spurting}} flow.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: either pattern can mean serious blood loss — rapid loss can quickly result in shock or even death.

Ex: signs of blood loss include active bleeding from a wound, or evidence such as blood on the clothes or near the patient.

Text: Blood is spurting from a deep cut on a chef's forearm. The flow pattern marks the bleeding as {{c1::arterial::arterial or venous}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: a large vein bleeds in a steady, even flow — serious, but without the spurts.

Text: When evaluating an {{c1::unconscious::responsive or unconscious}} patient, sweep for blood: run your gloved hands quickly and lightly {{c2::from head to toe}}, pausing periodically to {{c2::check your gloves for blood}}.
Back Extra:
Why: major blood loss is often visible as you approach — the glove sweep finds the bleeding that is not.

Pitfall: identify and control major external bleeding immediately; rapid blood loss can cause shock or even death.
verified_by: agent; husk_groups cleared: the visible sweep-for-blood scaffold cues both c2 spans — each is answerable with the other hidden

Text: The rapid exam — a head-to-toe sweep to identify life threats — is performed right after the {{c2::primary assessment::assessment phase}} and should take no more than {{c1::90}} seconds.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the rapid exam is not a focused assessment — it is a fast sweep for any additional injuries.

Why: injuries the sweep identifies must be managed prior to transport.

Text:
In the rapid exam you look and feel for DCAP-BTLS at every body region:

{{c1::Deformity::D}}

{{c1::Contusions::C}}

{{c1::Abrasions::A}}

{{c1::Punctures::P}}

{{c1::Burns::B}}

{{c1::Tenderness::T}}

{{c1::Lacerations::L}}

{{c1::Swelling::S}}
Back Extra:
Mnemonic: DCAP-BTLS — inspect and palpate for all eight findings at every stop of the head-to-toe sweep.

Why: the sweep exists to catch additional injuries that must be managed prior to transport.

Text:
Rapid exam, the head and the abdomen — the extra checks beyond DCAP-BTLS:

Head → also assess the {{c1::pupils}}

Abdomen → palpate for {{c1::rigidity (firm or soft)}} and {{c1::distention}}
Back Extra:
Why: a distended or firm abdomen can identify an internal hemorrhage — an indication for immediate transport.

Roster: rapid exam extras — head (pupils) → neck (JVD, tracheal deviation, spinal step-off) → chest (wall movement, crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, equal rise/fall + breath sounds) → abdomen (rigidity, distention) → pelvis (compress only if no pain) → extremities (distal pulses, motor, sensory) → back/buttocks (in-line roll, check before loading)

Text: Rapid exam, the pelvis — look for DCAP-BTLS; compress the pelvis only if the patient has {{c1::no pain::pain / no pain}}: palms over the {{c2::iliac crests::bony landmark}}, pressing gently {{c2::downward and inward::two directions}}, checking for tenderness and instability.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: pain at the pelvis means skip the compression — the squeeze is a test reserved for the pain-free pelvis.

Roster: rapid exam extras — head (pupils) → neck (JVD, tracheal deviation, spinal step-off) → chest (wall movement, crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, equal rise/fall + breath sounds) → abdomen (rigidity, distention) → pelvis (compress only if no pain) → extremities (distal pulses, motor, sensory) → back/buttocks (in-line roll, check before loading)

Text: A fall victim's rapid exam reaches the pelvis, and he winces with pain as you palpate it. Do you compress the iliac crests to test stability? {{c1::No::yes / no}}
Back Extra: Why: the compression test is gated on a pain-free pelvis — palpation pain is already a positive finding (the T in DCAP-BTLS).

Text: Rapid exam, the back and buttocks — in all trauma patients, roll the patient onto the side while maintaining {{c1::in-line stabilization of the spine::spine precaution}}, rolling in {{c1::one motion}}; check the back before you {{c2::load the patient for transport}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the one-motion roll is the log roll — spine held in line, a single smooth turn.

Roster: rapid exam extras — head (pupils) → neck (JVD, tracheal deviation, spinal step-off) → chest (wall movement, crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, equal rise/fall + breath sounds) → abdomen (rigidity, distention) → pelvis (compress only if no pain) → extremities (distal pulses, motor, sensory) → back/buttocks (in-line roll, check before loading)

Text: Distention is {{c1::swelling outward — being stretched or inflated}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Assess the abdomen, looking and palpating for DCAP-BTLS, rigidity (firm or soft), and distention."

Parts: dis- (apart) + tend- (stretch) — stretched apart.

Distinguish: rigidity = abnormal firmness of the abdominal wall; distention = abnormal swelling outward.

Text:
Rapid exam, the neck — beyond DCAP-BTLS, look and feel for:

{{c1::jugular venous distention (JVD)}}

{{c1::tracheal deviation from midline}}

{{c1::spinal step-off (a vertebra out of line with the rest)}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the neck's three extras follow its midline anatomy — vein, airway, spine.

Roster: rapid exam extras — head (pupils) → neck (JVD, tracheal deviation, spinal step-off) → chest (wall movement, crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, equal rise/fall + breath sounds) → abdomen (rigidity, distention) → pelvis (compress only if no pain) → extremities (distal pulses, motor, sensory) → back/buttocks (in-line roll, check before loading)

Text:
Rapid exam, the chest — beyond DCAP-BTLS there are four look/feel checks:

{{c1::chest wall movement}}

{{c1::crepitus}}

{{c1::subcutaneous emphysema}}

{{c1::equal rise and fall}}

…then {{c2::listen to breath sounds}} on both sides.
Back Extra:
Cue: eyes and hands do the four; the ears finish the chest.

Roster: rapid exam extras — head (pupils) → neck (JVD, tracheal deviation, spinal step-off) → chest (wall movement, crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, equal rise/fall + breath sounds) → abdomen (rigidity, distention) → pelvis (compress only if no pain) → extremities (distal pulses, motor, sensory) → back/buttocks (in-line roll, check before loading)

Text: Crepitus is {{c1::grating of broken bone ends rubbing together}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Assess the chest, looking and feeling for DCAP-BTLS, chest wall movement, crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, and equal rise and fall."

Distinguish: crepitus = bone-on-bone grating (felt or heard); subcutaneous emphysema = air crackling under the skin.

Parts: from Latin crepitare, "to crackle."

Formal: "a grating or grinding sensation or sound caused by fractured bone ends or joints rubbing together."

Text: Subcutaneous emphysema is {{c1::air trapped under the skin, felt as crackling}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Palpate the neck for signs of trauma … as well as a crackling sound produced by air bubbles under the skin, known as subcutaneous emphysema."

Distinguish: crepitus = bone-on-bone grating; subcutaneous emphysema = air crackling under the skin. And bare emphysema usually means the chronic lung disease (destroyed alveoli — a form of COPD); the subcutaneous form is a trauma finding.

Parts: sub- (under) + cutane- (skin) + emphysema (Greek: puffed up).

Formal: "a characteristic crackling sensation felt on palpation of the skin, caused by the presence of air in soft tissues."

Text:
Rapid exam, all four extremities — beyond DCAP-BTLS, assess bilaterally for:

{{c1::distal pulses}}

{{c1::motor function}}

{{c1::sensory function}}
Back Extra:
Cue: circulation, movement, feeling — each checked side against side.

Roster: rapid exam extras — head (pupils) → neck (JVD, tracheal deviation, spinal step-off) → chest (wall movement, crepitus, subcutaneous emphysema, equal rise/fall + breath sounds) → abdomen (rigidity, distention) → pelvis (compress only if no pain) → extremities (distal pulses, motor, sensory) → back/buttocks (in-line roll, check before loading)

Text:
Eight conditions make a patient high priority — transport immediately. The four that flag failing consciousness or ABCs:

{{c1::Unresponsive}}

{{c1::Altered LOC (level of consciousness)}}

{{c1::Difficulty breathing}}

{{c1::Uncontrolled bleeding}}
Back Extra:
Why: priority designation decides whether the patient gets immediate transport or can tolerate a few more minutes on scene.

Roster: high-priority conditions — unresponsive; difficulty breathing; uncontrolled bleeding; altered LOC; severe chest pain; pale skin or other signs of poor perfusion; complicated childbirth; severe pain in any area of the body

Text:
Eight conditions make a patient high priority — transport immediately. The other four, beyond consciousness and the ABCs:

{{c1::Severe chest pain}}

{{c1::Pale skin or other signs of poor perfusion}}

{{c1::Complicated childbirth}}

{{c1::Severe pain in any area of the body}}
Back Extra:
Cue: two are severe pain (chest, or anywhere), one is the skin announcing poor perfusion, one is a birth in trouble.

Roster: high-priority conditions — unresponsive; difficulty breathing; uncontrolled bleeding; altered LOC; severe chest pain; pale skin or other signs of poor perfusion; complicated childbirth; severe pain in any area of the body

visual_source.note: full 8-bullet list verified on the render; list ends on p977 (p978 opens the Golden Hour paragraph)

Text: A 45-year-old reports severe chest pain; his ABCs are intact and he is fully alert. Transport priority? {{c1::High — transport immediately::high / medium / low}}
Back Extra: Why: severe chest pain is on the high-priority list even with intact ABCs — priority designation asks whether he can tolerate a few more minutes on scene, and a high-priority patient cannot.

Text: {{c1::The Golden Hour}}, also called the {{c1::Golden Period}}, is the time from {{c2::injury}} to {{c2::definitive care}}, during which treatment of shock and traumatic injuries must occur to maximize the chance of survival.
Back Extra: Why: over time the body has increasing difficulty compensating for shock and traumatic injuries — so spend as little time as possible on scene in significant or severe trauma.
verified_by: agent; husk_groups cleared: the full definition stays visible as the anchor for both c1 names — an alias pair is one retrieval, not two mutually-dependent spans

Text: En route, reassess vital signs every {{c1::15}} minutes if the patient is stable, and every {{c1::5}} minutes (or as often as the situation permits) if unstable — until you reach the ED.
Back Extra:
Why: serial vitals reveal trends in the patient's condition — a single reading cannot.

Pitfall: do not be falsely reassured by apparently normal vital signs — the body compensates powerfully for severe injury or illness.

Text: Your patient's condition is worsening during transport, vitals trending down. How often do you reassess vital signs? {{c1::Every 5 minutes::interval}} — or as often as the situation permits.
Back Extra: Cue: unstable = every 5 min; stable = every 15 min — the unstable patient earns the tighter loop.

Text: Treating a patient for shock before {{c1::the blood pressure drops::vital-sign event}} increases the chance of survival.
Back Extra:
Why: even severe trauma can show fairly normal vitals at first; when compensation fails — decompensated shock — vitals deteriorate rapidly, especially in children.

Cue: the rapid fall at decompensation is exactly why vitals are rechecked so often.

visual_source.note: sparse page; wording verified on the render

Text: A motorcyclist has obvious severe trauma, but his vital signs are still fairly normal. When should you begin treating him for shock? {{c1::Immediately — before the blood pressure drops::right away / once BP falls}}
Back Extra: Why: normal early vitals can be compensation, not stability — treating before the pressure drops is what buys survival.

visual_source.note: sparse page; decision grounded in the marked sentence, wording verified on the render

Text: Two responders arrive at a scene with bystanders. To gather history without delaying care, one {{c1::questions the people in the vicinity}} while the other {{c1::initiates the patient assessment}}.
Back Extra:
Why: history from family, friends, and bystanders may be unobtainable once transport begins — collect it on scene.

Cue: also check for medical identification tags and paperwork about the events leading up.

Text: During history taking, a {{c1::symptom::sign or symptom}} is a problem or feeling the patient reports that others cannot feel or observe, while a {{c1::sign::sign or symptom}} is an objective condition that can be seen, heard, felt, smelled, or measured.
Back Extra: Ex: a patient saying he feels "weak" is giving you a symptom; visible bleeding or a measured blood pressure is a sign.

Text:
To explore the history of present illness — pain or any other symptom — the OPQRST questions cover:

{{c1::Onset::O}}

{{c1::Provocation/palliation::P}}

{{c1::Quality::Q}}

{{c1::Region/radiation::R}}

{{c1::Severity::S}}

{{c1::Timing::T}}
Back Extra:
Mnemonic: Onset — what were you doing when it began? Provocation/palliation — does anything make it better or worse; how are you most comfortable? Quality — sharp, dull, crushing, tearing; does it come in waves? Region/radiation — where is it; does it move anywhere? Severity — rate it on a 0-to-10 scale. Timing — how long have you had it; when did it start?

Cue: OPQRST is easiest for pain but adapts to dizziness, nausea, or shortness of breath.

visual_source.note: PARTIAL-grounded mark spans pages; all six elements, exact AAOS wording, and the 0-to-10 severity scale read from renders

Text: Your chest-pain patient says the pain eases when he sits up and leans forward — a detail that answers the {{c1::Provocation/palliation::OPQRST element}} element of OPQRST.
Back Extra:
Cue: anything that makes the symptom better or worse — including the position the patient is most comfortable in — answers P.

Distinguish: where the symptom is and whether it moves is Region/radiation, not P.

Text: In EMS assessment, pertinent negatives are {{c1::expected findings the patient does NOT have}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "sometimes just as important are the signs and symptoms that the patient does not have. These important negative findings are referred to as pertinent negatives."

Cue: a complaint usually brings related findings — chest pain is expected to come with shortness of breath; note when the expected partner is absent.

Formal: "negative findings that warrant no care or intervention."

Text:
A SAMPLE history gathers six kinds of information from the patient:

{{c1::Signs and symptoms::S}}

{{c1::Allergies::A}}

{{c1::Medications::M}}

{{c1::Pertinent past medical history::P}}

{{c1::Last oral intake::L}}

{{c1::Events leading up to the injury or illness::E}}
Back Extra:
Mnemonic: Signs and symptoms at the onset of the incident. Allergies — medication, food, or other substances, and the reactions; if none, chart "No known allergies." Medications — what is prescribed, at what dose and frequency; prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal taken in the last 12 hours; prescribed but not taken; recreational drugs. Pertinent past medical, surgical, or trauma history, plus important family history. Last oral intake — when and what. Events leading up — what led to the incident, and what happened between onset and your arrival.

Distinguish: OPQRST digs into the present symptom itself; SAMPLE frames the patient's whole history.

visual_source.note: PARTIAL-grounded mark spans pages; all six components, exact AAOS wording (P = Pertinent past medical history), and the 12-hour medication window read from renders

Text: In a woman of childbearing age, the L in a SAMPLE history stands for last oral intake and also {{c1::last menstrual period}}.
Back Extra: Pitfall: the second meaning adds a question — she is still asked about food and drink; the menstrual question comes on top of it.

Text: In EMS, cookbook medicine means {{c1::following the assessment steps without considering other options}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "it is important that [assessment] is not done robotically by the book. When providers do this, it is referred to as cookbook medicine — the process of going through steps in a process without considering other options."

Distinguish: the opposite of cookbook medicine is critical thinking — gathering, evaluating, and synthesizing information.

Why: EMS scenes are dynamic and often chaotic; a rote checklist misses what the scene is telling you.

Text: You should consider all women of {{c1::childbearing years::age group}} who report {{c1::lower abdominal pain::complaint}} to be {{c2::pregnant::working assumption}} unless ruled out by history or other information.
Back Extra: Pitfall: the follow-up questions touch her sexual history — never be judgmental, and everything gathered stays confidential except what treating her requires.

Text: A young adult woman reports cramping lower abdominal pain. Until history or other information rules it out, you work from the assumption that she is {{c1::pregnant}}.
Back Extra: Cue: childbearing years plus lower abdominal pain is the trigger pair — only history or other information can take the assumption away.

Text:
For a woman of childbearing years with lower abdominal pain, the pregnancy-status questions to ask cover:

her {{c1::last menstrual period}}

whether she {{c1::may be pregnant}}

any use of {{c1::birth control}}
Back Extra:
Cue: asked plainly — "When was your last menstrual period?" "Is there a possibility you may be pregnant?" "Are you using any form of birth control?"

Roster: the six questions for this scenario — last menstrual period · pads or tampons used, if bleeding · urinary frequency or burning · cramping severity and foul odors · possibility of pregnancy · birth control

Text:
For a woman of childbearing years with lower abdominal pain, the symptom questions to ask cover:

if she is bleeding — how many {{c1::sanitary pads or tampons}} she has used

any {{c1::urinary frequency or burning}}

the severity of her {{c1::cramping}}, and any {{c1::foul odors}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the pad-or-tampon count applies only if she is bleeding; the other questions are asked in every case.

Roster: the six questions for this scenario — last menstrual period · pads or tampons used, if bleeding · urinary frequency or burning · cramping severity and foul odors · possibility of pregnancy · birth control

Text:
When taking a male patient's history, you must inquire about urinary symptoms — the four questions cover:

{{c1::pain}} associated with urination

any {{c1::discharge, sores, or an increase in urination}}

{{c1::burning or difficulty voiding}}

whether there has been any {{c1::trauma}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the female lower-abdominal-pain set asks about urinary frequency or burning; the male set asks about burning or difficulty voiding.

Cue: when the presenting symptoms make it appropriate, also ask about the potential for sexually transmitted diseases.

Pitfall: never be judgmental about what you learn — sexual-history information is strictly confidential beyond what treatment requires.

Text: When a patient stays silent during history taking, consider whether the silence is itself a clue to the {{c1::chief complaint}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: a closed-ended question needing a simple yes or no may work best with a silent patient.

Ex: hunt for nonverbal clues — facial expressions showing pain or fear, how the patient sits or stands, or signs of a communication or language problem.

Text:
Some patients are overly talkative; possible causes include:

excessive {{c1::caffeine}} consumption

{{c1::nervousness}}

ingestion of {{c1::cocaine or methamphetamines}}

an underlying {{c1::psychological}} issue
Back Extra: Cue: after letting the patient express himself or herself, refocus — have the patient stick to the facts and clarify statements; there is no such thing as too much information.

Text: Pallor is {{c1::abnormally pale skin}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Some anxious patients exhibit signs of psychological shock, such as pallor, diaphoresis, shortness of breath, numbness in the hands and feet…"

Distinguish: pallor = white-pale skin (poor blood flow); cyanosis = blue-gray skin (poor oxygenation).

Cue: often accompanies severe bleeding and shock.

Text: Stroke, diabetes, trauma, medications, and other drugs can all alter the history a patient reports — but one of the most common causes of confusion is {{c1::hypoxia}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: never assume an older patient's confusion is dementia, delirium, or Alzheimer disease — confused behavior is not a normal response, so verify the patient's normal mental status.

Cue: once life threats are treated, ask about the chief complaint again, or ask someone close to the patient.

Text: A patient who was alert this morning now gives you a confused, contradictory history, and his blood glucose reads normal. One of the most common causes of confusion should make you check his {{c1::oxygenation::what to assess}}.
Back Extra: Why: hypoxia is one of the most common causes of confusion, so a newly muddled history may be the brain running short of oxygen.
verified_by: agent; R13 warning cleared: 'oxygenation' is the action-form paraphrase of the marked cause (hypoxia = too little oxygen) — the assessment implication the unit brief names as the auto-pair

Text: The purpose of the {{c1::secondary assessment::assessment phase}} is to perform {{c2::a systematic physical examination}} of the patient — done at the scene if the patient is stable, or en route to the hospital.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the primary assessment finds and treats immediate life threats — and it takes priority: there may be no time for a secondary assessment if life threats need continual management.

Cue: the exam may be head-to-toe or focused on one body area or system, guided by the chief complaint.

Text:
A physical examination uses three assessment techniques — name each from its description:

looking at the patient for abnormalities = {{c1::inspection}}

touching or feeling the patient for abnormalities = {{c1::palpation}}

listening to sounds the body makes, using a stethoscope = {{c1::auscultation}}
Back Extra:
Ex: auscultating a blood pressure — listening with a stethoscope to blood flow against the brachial artery as the cuff deflates.

Cue: DCAP-BTLS lists which abnormal findings to hunt for while inspecting and palpating each body region.

Text: When palpating, your {{c1::fingertips}} are best suited for detecting texture and consistency, while the {{c1::back of your hand}} is best suited for noting temperature.
Back Extra: Why: palpation pressure can be gentle or firmer to help pinpoint where the patient has pain.

Text: One ankle looks swollen, or one arm gives a grating sensation. Before you call such a finding abnormal, {{c1::compare it with the other side::action}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: breath sounds — always listen to both sides of the chest.

Cue: also sort out which findings are new and which are long-standing; do not assume a condition that causes discomfort just happened.

Text: {{c1::Battle sign::named sign}} is {{c2::bruising behind the ears}}, checked during the head portion of the full-body exam.
Back Extra: Cue: while at the ears, also use a penlight to check for drainage of spinal fluid or blood.

Text: The systematic full-body exam runs {{c1::head-to-toe::direction}} and finishes at the patient's {{c1::back::body region}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the back is reached by log rolling the patient — maintain spinal motion restriction if you suspect a spinal injury.

Pitfall: at the chest, look for obvious signs of injury before you begin palpating.

Text: A focused assessment is {{c1::an exam limited to the complaint's body part/system}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "A focused assessment is generally performed on patients who have sustained nonsignificant MOIs or on responsive medical patients."

Distinguish: the rapid full-body exam (significant MOI, unresponsive patients) sweeps head to toe and is NOT a focused assessment; the focused assessment targets one body part or system, guided by the chief complaint.

Formal: "a type of physical assessment typically performed on patients who have sustained nonsignificant mechanisms of injury or on responsive medical patients … based on the chief complaint and focuses on one body system or part."

Text: When examining a patient with a respiratory complaint, watch the exposed chest rise and fall to gauge {{c1::tidal volume::volume}}, along with the rate and effort of breathing.
Back Extra:
Cue: expose the chest, look again for signs of airway obstruction and for neck or chest trauma, and check that the right side looks like the left (symmetry).

Distinguish: retractions and accessory-muscle use speak to the effort (work) of breathing, not to its depth.

Text: High-pitched crowing sounds may indicate an upper airway obstruction from {{c1::a foreign body::cause}} — whereas stridor, a brassy crowing sound prominent on inspiration, suggests a partial occlusion caused by swelling.
Back Extra: Cue: both crowing sounds place the problem in the upper airway — the pitch and timing point to the likely cause.

Text: Mid-meal, a dinner guest abruptly develops high-pitched crowing sounds and struggles to breathe. Most likely cause? {{c1::Upper airway obstruction by a foreign body::impression}}
Back Extra:
Cue: sudden high-pitched crowing in someone who was just eating points to something lodged in the upper airway.

Distinguish: an upper airway narrowed by swelling produces stridor — a brassy crowing sound prominent on inspiration.

Text: Each complete breath has two phases — the {{c2::active::active or passive}} inhalation phase and the {{c2::passive::active or passive}} exhalation phase — occurring in a {{c1::1:3::ratio}} ratio over their duration.
Back Extra:
Why: during inhalation the diaphragm and intercostal muscles contract and the chest rises up and out; during exhalation the muscles relax and the chest returns to its original position.

Meaning: a 1:3 ratio means the inhalation phase lasts one-third as long as the exhalation phase.

Text:
You assess a patient's breathing in three ways:

watch {{c1::the chest rise and fall}}

listen to breath sounds with a stethoscope {{c1::over each lung::where}}

if the patient is {{c1::unconscious::which patients}}, feel for air at the mouth and nose during exhalation
Back Extra:
Why: breathing should normally be spontaneous and automatic — no conscious thought, visible effort, marked sounds, or pain.

Cue: 'each lung' matters — listen on both sides, not at a single spot.

Text:
When assessing breathing, you must obtain four pieces of information:

{{c1::Respiratory rate}}

{{c1::Rhythm (regular or irregular)}}

{{c1::Quality of breathing}}

{{c1::Depth of breathing}}
Back Extra: Ex: a complete report touches all four — '14 breaths/min, regular, quiet and clear, adequate depth.'

Text: Determine the respiratory rate by counting the patient's breaths for {{c1::30 seconds}} and {{c1::multiplying by two}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: count each breath at the same point in its cycle — peak chest rise is easiest, and a hand on the chest can feel what the eyes miss.

Pitfall: if the patient coughs, yawns, sighs, or talks during the count, wait a few seconds and start again.

Text: What is the normal respiratory rate, in breaths/min, for an adult at rest? {{c1::12 to 20::range}}
Back Extra: Why: resting values — the adult range follows the NHTSA education standards, and published ranges vary by source.

visual_source.note: adult range verified in prose on p1026 and in TABLE 10-4 on p1027

Text: A calm adult at rest is breathing 24 times/min, a rate {{c1::above::above/within/below}} the normal adult range.
Back Extra: Why: the normal adult resting range is 12 to 20 breaths/min — 24 is above its upper limit.

visual_source.note: tested range verified in prose and TABLE 10-4; the 24/min stem value is scenario dressing

Text: Count a conscious patient's respirations while still holding the wrist from the radial pulse — a patient aware of being evaluated will {{c1::override the automatic rate and depth::what happens}} of their breathing.
Back Extra:
Cue: count the chest rise you see or feel as the patient's forearm rises and falls with the chest.

Why: an aware patient usually breathes more slowly and deeply — so check respirations without letting the patient know what you are evaluating.

Text: What is the normal respiratory rate, in breaths/min, for an adolescent (13 to 18 years) at rest? {{c1::12 to 16::range}}
Back Extra: Why: resting values — pediatric ranges follow PALS, and published ranges vary by source.

visual_source.note: TABLE 10-4 row read from render

Text: What is the normal respiratory rate, in breaths/min, for a school-aged child (6 to 12 years) at rest? {{c1::18 to 30::range}}
Back Extra: Why: resting values — pediatric ranges follow PALS, and published ranges vary by source.

visual_source.note: TABLE 10-4 row read from render

Text: What is the normal respiratory rate, in breaths/min, for a preschooler (4 to 5 years) at rest? {{c1::22 to 34::range}}
Back Extra: Why: resting values — pediatric ranges follow PALS, and published ranges vary by source.

visual_source.note: TABLE 10-4 row read from render

Text: What is the normal respiratory rate, in breaths/min, for a toddler (1 to 3 years) at rest? {{c1::24 to 40::range}}
Back Extra: Why: resting values — pediatric ranges follow PALS, and published ranges vary by source.

visual_source.note: TABLE 10-4 row read from render (table spans p1027-p1028)

Text: What is the normal respiratory rate, in breaths/min, for an infant at rest? {{c1::30 to 60::range}}
Back Extra: Why: resting values — pediatric ranges follow PALS, and published ranges vary by source.

visual_source.note: TABLE 10-4 row read from render (table spans p1027-p1028)

Text: A 6-month-old resting quietly in a parent's arms breathes 45 times/min, a rate {{c1::within::above/within/below}} the normal infant range.
Back Extra:
Why: the normal infant range is 30 to 60 breaths/min — 45 sits comfortably mid-range.

Pitfall: a rate this fast would be abnormal in an adult; judge every rate against the patient's own age band.

visual_source.note: tested range verified in TABLE 10-4; the 45/min stem value is scenario dressing

Text: While counting respirations you also note the rhythm: when the timing between peak chest rises varies or the rate changes frequently, document the respirations as {{c1::irregular::regular or irregular}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: fairly consistent time from one peak chest rise to the next = regular respirations.

Cue: rhythm is judged while you count the rate, and regular vs irregular goes into the vital-signs documentation.

Text: Through a stethoscope, normal breath sounds are just air moving through the bronchi with a soft, {{c1::low::high or low}}-pitched murmur — clear, relatively quiet, and flowing freely in both inspiration and expiration.
Back Extra:
Cue: normal breathing is almost silent — in a quiet room you may hear only air movement at the mouth and nose.

Pitfall: breathing accompanied by any added sound points to a significant respiratory problem.
verified_by: agent; editor: 'free' -> 'flowing freely' (source: air moving freely)

Text: A snoring breath sound signals a simple but potentially dangerous upper airway obstruction — usually caused by the {{c1::tongue::structure}} (or a foreign body).
Back Extra:
Cue: snoring is an upper airway sound — no stethoscope is needed to hear it.

Distinguish: stridor is the other upper airway obstruction sound — harsh, brassy crowing from a foreign body or swelling, not the tongue.
verified_by: agent; parenthetical-after-cloze cleared: '(or a foreign body)' is the alternate cause from idx 135, not a definition or paraphrase of the hidden answer

Text: {{c1::Stridor::breath sound}} is a harsh, brassy, high-pitched crowing sound, most prominent on {{c2::inspiration::inspiration or expiration}}, from a partial obstruction of the {{c3::upper::upper or lower}} airway (foreign body or swelling).
Back Extra:
Cue: often heard before you even place a stethoscope — the obstruction sits in the neck or upper part of the chest.

Distinguish: wheezing is the lower-airway counterpart — a whistling sound most prominent on expiration.

Text: An adult with facial and neck swelling after a bee sting makes a harsh, brassy crowing sound each time she inhales. Name the sound and the level of the obstruction: {{c1::stridor::sound}}, from a partial {{c1::upper::upper or lower}} airway obstruction.
Back Extra:
Cue: crowing on inspiration plus a swelling mechanism at the neck or upper chest = stridor, not wheezing.

Pitfall: stridor is often audible before you even place a stethoscope — the presence of any abnormal breath sound already means an airway or breathing problem exists.
verified_by: agent; editor: Cue location matched to source (neck or upper part of the chest); Pitfall's unsupported 'do not wait to act' replaced with the source's own p1029 claim (any abnormal sound = airway/breathing problem exists)

Text: Bubbling or gurgling breath sounds mean there is fluid in the {{c1::upper airway::where}}, potentially impeding the exchange of gases.
Back Extra:
Why: suction the airway to clear it — this also reduces the risk of aspirating the fluid into the lungs.

Distinguish: crackles signal fluid deeper in the lungs (alveoli popping open), not pooled in the upper airway.

Text: {{c1::Crackles::breath sound}} are wet breath sounds like Rice Krispies added to milk — usually heard on both inspiration and expiration — that may indicate {{c2::fluid in the lungs::what, and where}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the crackling sound is made as the alveoli are popped open.

Distinguish: bubbling or gurgling is fluid up in the airway passages; crackles are fluid down at the alveoli.

Text: A choking restaurant patron goes silent — no cough, no speech, and you hear no breath sounds at all: he may be moving no air whatsoever. Your immediate priority: {{c1::clear the airway obstruction::action}}.
Back Extra:
Why: with a complete airway obstruction no air moves, so the patient can no longer cough or talk.

Pitfall: do not mistake total silence for quiet normal breathing — no sound may mean no air moving at all.

Text: {{c1::Wheezing::breath sound}} is a high-pitched whistling sound, most prominent on {{c2::expiration::inspiration or expiration}}, from obstruction or narrowing of the {{c3::lower::upper or lower}} airways.
Back Extra:
Cue: typically heard through auscultation (unlike stridor, which is often audible bare-eared) — and it points to a milder, lower-airway obstruction.

Distinguish: stridor = upper airway, brassy crowing, worst on inspiration.
verified_by: agent; editor: dropped unsupported 'only' (source: 'typically heard through auscultation')

Text: A patient who coughs up thick, yellow or green {{c2::sputum::term}} (matter from the lungs) most likely has {{c1::a respiratory infection::diagnosis}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: pink, frothy sputum points instead to a chest injury or congestive heart failure — an urgent cardiovascular-respiratory picture.
verified_by: agent; parenthetical-after-cloze cleared: '(matter from the lungs)' is the visible meaning cueing the describe-to-name direction of a definition — the licensed shape, not a leak (card-rules #3 precision); editor: spelled out CHF

Text: Coughing up pink, frothy sputum points to one of two causes: {{c1::a chest injury}} or {{c1::congestive heart failure}}.
Back Extra:
Why: with a chest injury, blood and fluid mix with air in the lungs — that patient may cough up frank blood or frothy white sputum too.

Pitfall: either cause means an urgent, potentially critical problem — anticipate oxygenation, ventilation, and rapid deterioration.
verified_by: agent; editor: 'and' -> 'or' ('one of two causes' + 'and' read incoherently; both members still hide together under c1)

Text: {{c1::Tidal volume::breathing measure}} is the amount of air moved into or out of the lungs during {{c2::one breath}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the depth of the breath is what determines whether tidal volume is normal, decreased, or increased.

Why: total air exchange depends on both the respiratory rate and the tidal volume.

Text: You can almost always hear breath sounds better from the patient's {{c1::back::front or back}} — auscultate there whenever it is accessible.
Back Extra: Cue: back not reachable → listen from the front and sides instead.

Text: Auscultate means {{c1::listen with a stethoscope}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "you can almost always hear a patient's breath sounds better from the patient's back; therefore, if the patient's back is accessible, listen (auscultate) there."

Cue: the noun form — auscultation — is also the standard way to measure a blood pressure, listening for Korotkoff sounds.

Parts: Latin auscultare, "to listen" (auris = ear).

Formal: "to listen to sounds within an organ with a stethoscope."

Text: To auscultate the upper lung fields (the {{c1::apices::term}}), place the stethoscope about {{c2::1 inch (2.5 cm)}} below the clavicle, at the {{c2::midclavicular}} line.
Back Extra: Pitfall: lift or go under clothing — over fabric you mostly hear the stethoscope sliding.

visual_source.note: landmark distance and line verified verbatim on render

Text: To auscultate the midlung fields, listen at the {{c1::third or fourth}} intercostal space, from the patient's {{c1::posterior::anterior or posterior}}.
Back Extra: Cue: the midlung field is the one auscultated from the back — where breath sounds are better heard anyway.

visual_source.note: intercostal-space numbers verified verbatim on render

Text: To auscultate the lower lung fields (the {{c1::bases::term}}), listen at the {{c2::sixth}} intercostal space, at the {{c2::midaxillary}} line.
Back Extra: Cue: listen on both sides of the chest at each location and compare left with right.

visual_source.note: intercostal-space number and line verified verbatim on render

Text: Place the {{c1::diaphragm::part of the stethoscope}} of the stethoscope firmly against {{c2::the skin::against skin or over clothing}} to hear breath sounds.
Back Extra: Why: lift the clothing or slide the stethoscope under it — listening over clothing, you mainly hear the stethoscope sliding on the fabric while the breath sounds are muted.
verified_by: agent; editor: c2 tightened to the crisp kernel 'the skin' (rule 5); the lift-or-slide method moved into the Why line (still 133's wording)

visual_source.note: PARTIAL-grounded mark 133 read in full across both renders; sentence confirmed verbatim

Text: {{c1::Rhonchi::breath sound}} are {{c2::low::high or low}}-pitched, congested breath sounds — like blowing bubbles under water, most prominent on expiration — suggesting mucus or fluid in the lungs, often with a productive cough.
Back Extra: Distinguish: wheezing is a high-pitched whistle from narrowed lower airways; crackles are wet cracklings of fluid at the alveoli — rhonchi are the low, congested ones, from mucus.

Text:
The quality (character) of a patient's respirations can be described in one of four ways:

{{c1::Normal}}

{{c1::Shallow}}

{{c1::Labored}}

{{c1::Noisy}}
Back Extra: Cue: judge the character while you count the rate — by ear, or better, by auscultating with a stethoscope.
