Text:
A patient's chief complaint is located in the chest — carefully reevaluate the:

{{c1::pulse rate}}

{{c1::skin}}

{{c1::blood pressure}}

{{c1::breath sounds}}

Then inspect and palpate from the {{c2::clavicles}} to the shoulder to the {{c2::abdomen}}.
Back Extra:
Why: a complaint located in the chest implicates the cardiovascular and respiratory systems together, so the perfusion findings get rechecked alongside the lungs.

Cue: note and document every abnormality you find — the findings drive the treatment plan and the transport priority.

Text: Once you determine that a pulse is present, judge its adequacy by assessing pulse {{c1::rate}}, pulse {{c1::quality}}, and pulse {{c1::rhythm}}.
Back Extra: Cue: for a chest-pain complaint, the pulse, respiratory rate, and blood pressure each deserve particular attention to rate, quality, and rhythm.

Text: To judge how well the cardiovascular system is functioning, check the {{c1::distal::proximal/distal}} pulses and compare them for right- and left-side differences.
Back Extra:
Cue: skin condition findings pair with the pulse exam to show how well the cardiovascular and respiratory systems are working.

Pitfall: a chief complaint in the chest may have a medical cause or be the result of trauma — don't anchor on one.

Text: Beyond breath sounds, you may also consider auscultating the chest-pain patient for abnormal {{c1::heart sounds}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: breath sounds are listened for as a standard part of the chest exam; heart sounds are only a consider step.

Pitfall: a noisy prehospital setting can make heart sounds difficult to obtain.

Text: What is the normal pulse-rate range for adults and children older than 10 years, in beats/min? {{c1::60 to 100::range}}
Back Extra: Cue: well-conditioned athletes and patients on heart medications such as beta blockers may run considerably lower — you can always ask patients whether they know their normal resting rate.

visual_source.note: range read from the TABLE 10-6 render; the extractor's context text for this table is garbled

Text: What is the normal pulse-rate range for preschoolers and school-aged children (2 to 10 years), in beats/min? {{c1::60 to 140::range}}
Back Extra: Why: in general, the younger the pediatric patient, the faster the pulse rate.

visual_source.note: range read from the TABLE 10-6 render; the extractor's context text for this table is garbled

Text: What is the normal pulse-rate range for infants and toddlers (3 months to 2 years), in beats/min? {{c1::100 to 190::range}}
Back Extra: Why: pediatric pulse rates generally run faster the younger the child.

visual_source.note: range read from the TABLE 10-6 render; the extractor's context text for this table is garbled

Text: What is the normal pulse-rate range for infants up to 3 months of age, in beats/min? {{c1::85 to 205::range}}
Back Extra: Meaning: the normal pediatric pulse-rate ranges come from the AHA's Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS, 2015) data.

visual_source.note: range read from the TABLE 10-6 render; the extractor's context text for this table is garbled

Text: To obtain the pulse rate in most patients, count the pulses felt in a {{c1::30-second}} period and then multiply by {{c1::two}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: respirations are counted the same way (30 seconds × 2) — know which vital sign is being asked about.

Pitfall: a weak, irregular, or extremely slow pulse breaks the rule — count it for a full minute.

Text:
Count the pulse for {{c1::a full minute::duration}} when it is:

{{c2::weak and difficult to palpate}}

{{c2::irregular}}

{{c2::extremely slow}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: most patients get 30 seconds × 2; a weak, irregular, or extremely slow pulse earns the full 60-second count.

Why: faint, uneven, or very slow beats make a half-minute sample unreliable — the full minute captures the true rate.

Text: Your patient's radial pulse is faint under your fingers, and the beats arrive at uneven intervals. How long should you count this pulse? {{c1::A full minute (60 seconds)::duration}}
Back Extra:
Cue: weak-and-difficult, irregular, or extremely slow → a full-minute count.

Distinguish: a strong, regular pulse gets the usual 30 seconds × 2.

Text:
Report pulse quality with the standard terms:

feels normal under your fingers → describe it as {{c1::strong}}

noticeably more forceful than normal → {{c1::bounding}}

weak and difficult to feel → weak or {{c1::thready}}
Back Extra:
Why: the pulse is taken where it is normally strong and easy to feel — the radial or carotid artery in adults, the brachial artery in infants — so a pulse of normal strength reports as 'strong.'

Cue: report the quality every time you report or record a pulse.

Text: Your patient's radial pulse forcefully snaps against your fingertips with each beat — far easier to feel than a typical pulse. Report this pulse quality as {{c1::bounding::quality term}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: 'bounding' is the practitioners' term for a stronger-than-normal pulse.

Distinguish: the opposite finding — weak and difficult to feel — is reported as 'weak' or 'thready.'

Text: A pulse rhythm is irregular when the heart periodically has an {{c1::early}} or {{c1::late}} beat, or {{c1::misses}} a beat.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: rhythm is about the interval between beats — regardless of the rate, equal intervals are documented as regular.

Why: an irregular pulse in a patient with cardiovascular signs and symptoms likely needs advanced cardiac assessment — per protocol: ALS backup, a paramedic intercept, or prompt transport.

Cue: when possible, find out whether the irregularity is new or a chronic or normal condition for the patient.

Text:
A decrease in blood pressure may indicate one of 3 problems:

{{c1::loss of blood or its fluid components}}

{{c1::loss of vascular tone / insufficient arterial constriction (even without any fluid loss)}}

{{c1::a cardiac pumping problem}}
Back Extra:
Why: pressure needs fluid to push, vessels that squeeze, and a working pump — one failure mode for each.

Cue: compensation (faster heart rate + arterial constriction) can hold the pressure normal at first, whichever cause is at work.

Text: A decreased blood pressure is a {{c1::late::early/late}} sign of shock — the patient is in the {{c1::decompensated::compensated/decompensated}} stage.
Back Extra:
Meaning: decompensated = the critical stage; the compensatory mechanisms can no longer hold the pressure up.

Pitfall: a normal blood pressure never rules out shock — it may be compensation doing the work.

Mechanism: falling circulation → faster heart rate + arterial constriction → skin and extremity flow shunted to the vital organs → BP stays normal until the defenses fail.

Text: A man vomiting blood has kept a rapid pulse with a normal BP; on reassessment his blood pressure begins to fall. The falling BP means he has entered {{c1::decompensated (critical-stage) shock::stage}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the falling pressure marks the moment the compensating heart rate and vasoconstriction can no longer keep up.

Cue: any markedly low BP means vital-organ perfusion is inadequate — pressure and perfusion must be restored to normal.

Text: Some people have chronically high blood pressure caused by {{c1::progressive narrowing of the arteries::vascular change}} that comes with age.
Back Extra: Ex: during an acute episode, a chronically hypertensive patient's pressure can climb even higher than the already-high baseline.

Text: A serious head injury can push the blood pressure {{c1::very high::very high/very low}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: markedly elevated pressure in a trauma patient should raise your suspicion of head injury.

Distinguish: age-related arterial narrowing raises BP chronically — a head injury can spike it acutely.

Text: Abnormally high blood pressure may cause {{c1::a rupture (or other critical damage)::consequence}} in the arterial system.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: low BP starves the vital organs (perfusion failure); very high BP threatens the vessels themselves.

Cue: when pressure climbs, the body's own defenses act to bring it back down.

Text: {{c1::Systolic pressure::BP component}} is {{c2::the arterial pressure surge with each ventricular contraction}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: systole = the ventricles' contraction phase.

Cue: each surge IS the pulse wave you palpate at the wrist.

Distinguish: diastolic pressure is the residual floor while the heart relaxes.

Text: {{c1::Diastolic pressure::BP component}} is {{c2::the residual arterial pressure while the heart relaxes}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: diastole = the relaxing phase of the heart's cycle, when the left ventricle is at rest.

Cue: 'residual' — the floor never drains to zero between beats.

Distinguish: systolic pressure is the surge with each contraction.

Text: {{c1::Systolic}} pressure represents the {{c2::maximum::maximum/minimum}} pressure the arteries are subjected to, and {{c1::diastolic}} pressure represents the {{c2::minimum::maximum/minimum}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: blood pressure swings between a ceiling and a floor — the two names label the edges of that swing.

Why: the diastolic minimum never drains away — some pressure is always present in the arteries between beats.

Text: Blood pressure is measured in {{c1::millimeters of mercury (mm Hg)::unit}}.
Back Extra: Cue: the sphygmomanometer's gauge and your PCR entry use the same unit.

Text:
A patient's systolic pressure is 120 and diastolic pressure is 80. Give the reading two ways:

recorded on the PCR: {{c1::"BP 120/80 mm Hg"::written form}}

reported aloud: {{c1::"120 over 80"::spoken form}}
Back Extra:
Why: blood pressure is reported as a fraction — always systolic over diastolic.

Cue: the spoken form drops the unit; the written form keeps mm Hg.

Text:
Before cuffing an arm for a BP, check for 4 named reasons to use the other arm instead:

{{c1::a dialysis fistula}}

{{c1::central lines / an IV site}}

{{c1::a mastectomy on that side}}

{{c1::an injury to that arm}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the check ends with a catch-all — "or other reason not to use this arm"; when in doubt, switch.

Ex: a dialysis patient with chronic renal failure — ask about a fistula before the cuff goes on.

Text: A mastectomy is {{c1::surgical removal of a breast}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Avoid obtaining a blood pressure reading on an arm if the patient … has had a mastectomy on that side; or has an injury to that arm."

Why: after a mastectomy, do not take a blood pressure on that side's arm — ask if it is not visible.

Parts: mast- (breast) + -ectomy (surgical removal).

Text: In dialysis patients, a fistula is {{c1::a surgically made vein-to-artery connection}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Avoid obtaining a blood pressure reading on an arm if the patient has an intravenous site or other medical device in place, such as an indwelling catheter or dialysis fistula…"

Why: never take a blood pressure on the fistula arm — ask dialysis patients which arm to avoid.

Parts: Latin fistula, "pipe / tube."

Formal: "a surgically created connection between a vein and an artery," usually located in the forearm or upper arm.

Text: A normal-size BP cuff is designed to wrap around the arm {{c1::1 to 1.5}} times and take up {{c1::two-thirds::fraction}} of the length from the armpit to the elbow crease.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a cuff too SMALL reads falsely high; a cuff too LARGE reads falsely low.

Cue: most agencies carry at least three sizes — thigh, adult, and pediatric (plus a large adult).

Text: A thigh cuff goes on the arm of patients who are {{c1::obese}} or have {{c1::exceptionally well-developed arm muscles}} — and it takes a thigh BP when {{c1::both arms are injured}}.
Back Extra:
Why: an oversized arm makes the standard cuff effectively too small — and a too-small cuff reads falsely high.

Distinguish: the small pediatric cuff covers children and exceptionally small adults.

Cue: measure a blood pressure in every patient older than 3 years.

Text: In BP auscultation, the inflated cuff compresses the {{c1::brachial}} artery; the turbulence and arterial vibrations it creates are heard as {{c1::Korotkoff::eponym}} sounds. As the cuff is released, the sounds {{c2::appear::appear/disappear}} at the systolic pressure and {{c2::disappear::appear/disappear}} at the diastolic.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: squeezed artery → turbulent flow as blood first returns (sound = systolic); once the artery is fully open the flow runs smooth and silent (silence = diastolic).

Cue: stethoscope over the brachial artery while the cuff bleeds down.

Text: Very fit people and patients taking {{c1::beta blockers::drug class}} may have a normal resting heart rate below {{c1::60}} beats/min.
Back Extra: Cue: ask patients their usual pulse and blood pressure — many track heart rate on a smart watch and know their baseline.

Text: A 24-year-old triathlete who feels fine after a minor wrist injury has a resting pulse of 52 beats/min, strong and regular. Most likely explanation: {{c1::a normal variant for a very fit person::normal variant or warning sign}}.
Back Extra:
Why: a very fit person's normal resting rate can sit below 60 beats/min.

Cue: beta blockers produce the same slow-but-normal resting rate — ask about medications and the patient's known baseline.

Text: Measuring BP by palpation uses the cuff plus your fingers on the {{c1::radial::pulse site}} pulse (no stethoscope), and it yields only the {{c1::systolic::systolic/diastolic}} pressure — the other component cannot be determined.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: once you find the pulse, do not move your fingertips until the measurement is done.

Distinguish: auscultation (stethoscope over the brachial artery) yields both pressures.

Cue: either method, the cuff's distal edge sits about 1 in (2.5 cm) above the elbow crease (antecubital space), arm held at heart level.

Text: Inflate the BP cuff until the pulse (or its sounds) disappears, then continue up to {{c1::200}} mm Hg before starting the slow release.
Back Extra:
Why: overshooting guarantees the cuff starts above the systolic point, so the first returning tap or pulse is the true systolic.

Cue: the same 200 mm Hg target applies by auscultation and by palpation.

Text: As a BP cuff deflates, the gauge needle often bounces in time with the pulsation — those needle movements {{c1::are not::are/are not}} the patient's blood pressure.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: with a very low BP, the sounds can continue all the way down — record the diastolic as "0" (heard until the gauge read 0).

Cue: pressures come from the sounds (or the returning pulse), never from needle motion.

recorded on the PCR: {{c1::"120/P"::written form}}

Cue: document the time, and note that the pressure was taken by palpation.

Text:
Perform a neurologic assessment anytime a patient shows one of six trigger presentations. Four are ongoing states:

{{c1::changes in mental status}}

{{c1::stupor}}

{{c1::drowsiness}}

{{c1::dizziness}}
Back Extra:
Why: the assessment can begin hands-off — simply talking with the patient during the primary assessment already tests mental status.

Roster: changes in mental status · stupor · drowsiness · dizziness · possible head injury · syncope

Text:
Perform a neurologic assessment anytime a patient shows one of six trigger presentations. Two are discrete events:

{{c1::a possible head injury}}

{{c1::syncope}}
Back Extra:
Cue: "anytime you are confronted with" one of the six — syncope still counts even after the patient seems fully recovered.

Roster: changes in mental status · stupor · drowsiness · dizziness · possible head injury · syncope

Text: A man briefly fainted at church; by the time you arrive he is awake, oriented, and joking. His syncope alone still calls for a {{c1::neurologic::assessment type}} assessment.
Back Extra:
Why: syncope is one of the six standing triggers — a normal-looking recovery does not remove it.

Cue: start simple — talking, asking questions, and getting an appropriate reply already begins the assessment.

Text: The diameter and reactivity to light of a patient's pupils can reflect the status of the {{c1::brain::organ}} — its perfusion, oxygenation, and overall condition.
Back Extra: Why: pupil size is set from inside the skull by continuous automatic commands, so an organ in trouble up there can show itself in the eyes.

Text:
A healthy patient's pupils adjust their size to the available light:

In normal room light → {{c1::about midsize::size}}

With less light → {{c1::dilate::dilate/constrict}}

With a bright light shined near the eye → {{c1::constrict::dilate/constrict}}

In the absence of light → {{c1::fully relaxed and dilated::dilated/constricted}}
Back Extra:
Why: dilation lets more light into the eye — and normally pupil size changes instantly with any change in light level.

Pitfall: some patients' pupils do not react properly because of eye surgery or other conditions — confirm with the patient or family before reading meaning into it.
verified_by: agent; fragment_clozed_list cleared: keyed condition-to-response panel (recipes §8 direction-of-change shape) — each row hides the ENTIRE answer cued by its visible light condition, not a filler word in a reproducible frame

Text: When a brighter light is introduced into one eye only, {{c1::both::one/both}} pupils should constrict {{c1::equally::equally/unequally}}.
Back Extra: Why: the brain sets the two pupils to the appropriate size for the pupil receiving the most light.

Text: You shine a penlight into a patient's right eye and watch her left pupil constrict as well. The motor command that reached that left eye traveled from the brain through the {{c1::oculomotor::cranial nerve}} nerves.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the light level travels TO the brain as sensory signals from each eye; the constriction order travels FROM the brain through the oculomotor nerves.

Cue: light in one eye sizes both pupils — the brain commands each eye together.

Text: Pupil size is regulated by continuous motor commands that the brain automatically sends through the {{c1::oculomotor::cranial nerve}} nerves to each eye, constricting both pupils to the same appropriate size.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: each eye first sends sensory signals to the brain reporting its light level; the oculomotor commands are the brain's motor reply to each eye.

Cue: oculo- (eye) + motor (movement command) — the name says exactly what the nerves carry.

Text: {{c1::Anisocoria::pupil term}} is {{c2::normally unequal pupils}}, found in a small number of patients.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: unequal pupils count as "normal for the patient" only if the patient or a family member can confirm it — otherwise presume altered brain function from CNS depression or injury.

Parts: an- (not) + iso- (equal) + cor- (pupil) — pupils not equal.

Text: After a fall, an older patient's pupils react sluggishly to your penlight and the left is larger than the right. No one can confirm a preexisting eye condition, so you should presume the abnormal response indicates {{c1::altered brain function (from CNS depression or injury)::significance}}.
Back Extra:
Why: pupil size is driven by the brain, so an unexplained abnormal response is treated as a brain problem until proven otherwise.

Cue: "normal for the patient" only counts when the patient or family can confirm it.

Text:
Of the five abnormal pupil findings that indicate altered brain function, three are ways the reaction to light goes wrong:

{{c1::become fixed — no reaction at all (whether dilated or constricted)}}

{{c1::react backward — dilate when a bright light is introduced, constrict when it is removed}}

{{c1::react sluggishly instead of briskly}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: before calling a response abnormal, ask about eye surgery or other conditions that make odd pupils normal for this patient.

Roster: fixed (no reaction) · backward (dilate with light) · sluggish · unequal in size · unequal when light is introduced into or removed from one eye

Text: Two of the five abnormal pupil findings are not about how the pupils react — pupils that become {{c1::unequal in size::finding}}, at rest or {{c1::when a bright light is introduced into or removed from one eye::triggering moment}}, also indicate altered brain function.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a small number of patients have anisocoria — normally unequal pupils; inequality is presumed abnormal only when no one can confirm it as the patient's baseline.

Roster: fixed (no reaction) · backward (dilate with light) · sluggish · unequal in size · unequal when light is introduced into or removed from one eye

Text:
Causes of depressed brain function — the state abnormal pupils can reveal — include three structural ones:

{{c1::injury of the brain or brainstem}}

{{c1::trauma or stroke}}

{{c1::a brain tumor}}
Back Extra:
Cue: "some of the causes include" — an open set; these named ones are the classics, not an exhaustive list.

Roster: injury of the brain or brainstem · trauma or stroke · brain tumor · inadequate oxygenation or perfusion · drugs or toxins (CNS depressants)

Text:
Causes of depressed brain function — the state abnormal pupils can reveal — include two nonstructural ones:

{{c1::inadequate oxygenation or perfusion}}

{{c1::drugs or toxins (central nervous system depressants)}}
Back Extra:
Why: the brain fails without oxygen and blood flow even when nothing is structurally wrong — and CNS depressants turn it down chemically.

Roster: injury of the brain or brainstem · trauma or stroke · brain tumor · inadequate oxygenation or perfusion · drugs or toxins (CNS depressants)

Text:
In pupil assessment, the mnemonic PEARRL stands for:

{{c1::Pupils::P}}

{{c1::Equal::E}}

{{c1::And::A}}

{{c1::Round::R}}

{{c1::Regular in size::R}}

{{c1::React to Light::L}}
Back Extra: Cue: the two R's are different checks — Round is the shape, Regular in size is the size; the A is just "And."

visual_source.note: letter-by-letter expansion table read from render

Text: When a patient's pupil check is entirely normal, you can report it with the single mnemonic — "Pupils = {{c1::PEARRL}}" — while any abnormal finding must instead be {{c2::described using the longer form}}.
Back Extra: Ex: abnormal long form — "Pupils are equal and round, the left pupil is fixed and dilated, the right pupil is regular in size and reacts to light."

Text:
To assess neurovascular status in an injured extremity, check four components:

{{c1::pulse}}

{{c1::capillary refill}}

{{c1::sensation}}

{{c1::motor function}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the check runs circulation first (pulse, capillary refill), then nerve supply (sensation), then movement (motor function).

Pitfall: sensory and motor checks require patient cooperation — they cannot be assessed in an unconscious patient.

Text:
In a neurovascular check, palpate the pulse {{c2::distal::distal or proximal}} to the point of injury:

Upper extremity → the {{c1::radial}} pulse

Lower extremity → the {{c1::posterior tibial}} and {{c1::dorsalis pedis}} pulses
Back Extra:
Cue: assess the lower-extremity pulses for rate, quality, and rhythm — fast, slow, or irregular? weak, thready, or bounding?

Pitfall: pale or cyanotic skin in a hand or foot may mean poor circulation in that extremity.

Text:
In the neurovascular exam, check hand sensation by light touch at three spots:

{{c1::the flesh near the index fingertip}}

{{c1::the thumb}}

{{c1::the little finger}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: an unconscious patient cannot report light touch, so this check needs a cooperative patient.

Roster: light-touch sites — hand: index fingertip · thumb · little finger; foot: flesh of the big toe · lateral side of the foot.

Text:
In the neurovascular exam, check foot sensation by light touch at two spots:

{{c1::the flesh of the big toe}}

{{c1::the lateral side of the foot}}

A patient who senses light touch in the fingers or toes distal to a fracture most likely has {{c2::an intact nerve supply::what it indicates}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: sensation sites are skin flesh (fingertips, big toe, lateral foot); pulse sites are vessels (radial, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis) — don't blur the two lists.

Roster: light-touch sites — hand: flesh near the index fingertip · thumb · little finger; foot: flesh of the big toe · lateral side of the foot.

Text: In the capillary refill test, press the tip of the fingernail or toenail until the skin blanches (turns white). If normal color does not return within {{c1::2 seconds}} of releasing the nail, assume {{c2::circulation is impaired::conclusion}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the test is typically recommended for use in children, although it can also be used in adults.

Cue: before pressing, note and record the skin color — any pallor or cyanosis.

Text: In the motor check of an injured limb (open and close a fist; wiggle the toes and move the foot up and down), if an attempted motion produces {{c1::pain}} at the injury site, stop that part of the exam — and skip the motor test entirely when the injury involves the {{c2::hand or foot}} itself.
Back Extra:
Why: the motions are performed by the hand or foot, so testing an injured hand or foot itself would cause pain — the test is meant for injuries proximal to them.

Cue: fist = upper extremity; toes and foot up-and-down = lower extremity.

Text: You are assessing a 6-year-old's splinted forearm. You press her fingernail until it blanches; after release, normal color takes about 4 seconds to return. Conclusion? {{c1::Circulation in that limb is impaired::circulation judgment}}
Back Extra:
Why: normal color must return within 2 seconds of releasing the nail — 4 seconds is delayed.

Cue: capillary refill testing is typically recommended for use in children.

Text: An ecchymosis is {{c1::a bruise — blood pooled under the skin}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Is there evidence of trauma, such as ecchymoses or hematomas?"

Distinguish: a hematoma is a raised pocket of collected blood; an ecchymosis is flat discoloration.

Parts: ec- (out) + chym- (juice) + -osis (condition) — blood leaked out into the skin.

Formal: "a buildup of blood beneath the skin that produces a characteristic blue or black discoloration as the result of an injury."

Text: Paradoxical motion is {{c1::one chest section moving opposite the rest}} during breathing.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Observe for abnormal breathing signs, including retractions or paradoxical motion (when only one section of the chest rises on inspiration while another area of the chest falls)."

Why: the flail segment is detached, so it sinks in on inhalation while the rest of the chest expands.

Distinguish: retractions = skin pulling in around the ribs from impaired airflow (usually medical); paradoxical motion = a rib-fracture segment moving opposite (trauma).

Formal: "the motion — in during inhalation, out during exhalation — is exactly the opposite of normal chest wall motion."

Text: A flail (flail chest) is {{c1::a chest-wall segment broken free, moving independently}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Paradoxical motion is associated with a fracture of several ribs (flail), causing a section of the chest to move independently from the rest of the chest wall."

Cue: the telltale sign of a flail is paradoxical motion — the free segment moves opposite the rest of the chest.

Formal: "a condition in which two or more adjacent ribs are fractured in two or more places or in association with a fracture of the sternum so that a segment of the chest wall is effectively detached from the rest of the thoracic cage."
verified_by: agent; editor re-verified the p4057 glossary quote via pdftotext

Text: A pneumothorax is {{c1::air in the space around a lung}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Palpate the chest for subcutaneous emphysema, especially in cases of severe blunt chest trauma, as this could indicate a pneumothorax."

Parts: pneumo- (air) + thorax (chest) — air loose in the chest.

Distinguish: subcutaneous emphysema is air under the SKIN; a pneumothorax is air INSIDE the chest around the lung — finding the first should make you suspect the second.

Formal: "an accumulation of air or gas in the pleural cavity."

Text: On abdominal exam, guarding is {{c1::the belly wall involuntarily tensing against pain}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Palpate the abdomen for tenderness, rigidity, and patient guarding."

Distinguish: rigidity = the wall staying board-firm; guarding = muscles tensing up in response to movement or touch.

Formal: "involuntary muscle contractions (spasm) of the abdominal wall to minimize the pain of abdominal movement; a sign of peritonitis."

Text:
Report abdominal palpation findings using four descriptors:

{{c1::firm}}

{{c1::soft}}

{{c1::tender}}

{{c1::distended}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: distended = swollen.

Cue: palpate for tenderness, rigidity, and guarding — and if the patient is awake and alert, ask about pain as you examine.

Text: A patient reports sharp pain in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. In which quadrant do you begin palpating? {{c1::The left upper quadrant (LUQ)::quadrant}}
Back Extra: Why: palpation always starts in the quadrant farthest from the pain — for RLQ pain, the diagonal opposite is the LUQ.

Text: Always start palpation of the abdomen in the quadrant {{c1::farthest from::farthest from or closest to}} the patient's pain.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: do not palpate obvious soft-tissue injuries, and be careful not to palpate too firmly.

Cue: the four quadrants are the LUQ, LLQ, RUQ, and RLQ.

Text: When a patient reports no pelvic pain, apply gentle pressure to the pelvis — never {{c1::rock::motion}} it.
Back Extra:
Why: rocking can worsen (exacerbate) damage to any unstable bones.

Pitfall: pelvic and surrounding abdominal injuries can bleed profusely with no obvious external signs — keep monitoring mental status, skin condition, and vital signs.

Cue: any movement, crepitus, or reported pain or tenderness on gentle pressure = possible severe injury.

Text: When evaluating the extremities, always compare the {{c1::right side with the left side}}, looking for weakness or atrophy, and assess {{c1::equality::what property}} of grip strength.
Back Extra: Cue: ask how much the patient can move each extremity or joint — never force a painful joint to move.

Text: Pulse oximetry evaluates the effectiveness of {{c1::oxygenation::oxygenation or ventilation}}. The pulse oximeter is a {{c1::photoelectric::device type}} device that monitors the {{c1::oxygen saturation of hemoglobin}} in the capillary beds.
Back Extra:
Meaning: hemoglobin = the iron-containing part of the red blood cell that oxygen attaches to.

Pitfall: a monitoring device is an adjunct — it never replaces your comprehensive assessment of the patient.

Cue: normal ambient-air values mostly fall between 94% and 99%, varying with altitude.

Text: Because the pulse oximeter's light source must have unobstructed access to a capillary bed, {{c1::dark fingernail polish}} might need to be removed before clipping on the probe.
Back Extra:
Why: the sensing probe clips onto a finger or earlobe and shines light through the capillary bed — anything opaque over the nail corrupts the reading.

Cue: results appear as a percentage on the display screen.

Text: A pulse oximeter functions properly only with adequate {{c1::perfusion}} and adequate numbers of {{c1::red blood cells::blood component}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the sensor reads blood in a capillary bed — vasoconstriction empties the bed, and lost red cells leave less hemoglobin to read.

Pitfall: never let a good-looking SpO2 number prevent oxygen for a patient who reports difficulty breathing.

Text: A patient in shock has pale, cool skin. The monitor shows SpO2 99%. That value may be {{c1::inaccurate or misleading::trust judgment}}.
Back Extra:
Why: shock causes vasoconstriction, and the pulse oximeter needs an adequately perfused capillary bed (and enough red blood cells) to read accurately.

Pitfall: bleeding and anemia break the reading the same way — too few red blood cells to read.

Text: A pulse oximeter presumes {{c1::oxygen}} is what saturates the hemoglobin, so any chemical that {{c1::displaces oxygen}} — such as {{c1::carbon monoxide::toxic gas}} — may cause misleading values.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the pulse oximeter is only a tool — not a substitute for a good assessment.

Distinguish: low-perfusion states (vasoconstriction, blood loss) break the reading differently — too little capillary blood to read, versus the wrong chemical riding the hemoglobin.

Text: During a winter power outage, two adults are found barely responsive in a home where a charcoal grill has been burning indoors. The monitor shows SpO2 98%, but the reading cannot be trusted because inhaled {{c1::carbon monoxide::gas}} may have {{c1::displaced the oxygen}} on their hemoglobin.
Back Extra: Cue: the oximeter only presumes oxygen is what saturates hemoglobin — it cannot tell which chemical is actually aboard.

Text: {{c1::Capnography::monitoring method}} is a {{c2::noninvasive}} method that quickly and efficiently provides information on a patient's {{c2::ventilation}}, {{c2::circulation}}, and {{c2::metabolism}}.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: oxygen burns the fuel of metabolism and carbon dioxide is the exhaust — capnography measures that exhaust in exhaled air.

Distinguish: pulse oximetry shows how much oxygen is available to the cells; measuring exhaled CO2 shows how much is being used.

Cue: monitors attach to the end of an advanced airway or onto a nasal cannula.

Text: Waveform capnography shows a graph of how {{c1::easily}}, how {{c1::frequently}}, and how {{c1::much}} the patient is exhaling carbon dioxide.
Back Extra: Cue: capnography is used to evaluate breathing treatments and artificial ventilation and to confirm endotracheal tube placement; it correlates with lactic acid values in septic shock.

Text:
Check a blood glucose level in three patient groups:

all patients {{c1::known to have diabetes}}

all patients with {{c1::an altered mental status}}

patients with {{c1::generalized malaise or weakness}}
Back Extra:
Cue: in addition, a blood glucose level can be assessed in any patient you think has a poor general impression.

Why: a low level can explain why a patient is unresponsive; a high level with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and a mental-status change may signal dangerous complications of high blood glucose.

Text: A 58-year-old has no specific complaint — he just feels weak all over. What bedside level should you assess? {{c1::Blood glucose}}
Back Extra: Why: generalized malaise or weakness is one of the three standing indications for glucometry, alongside known diabetes and altered mental status.

Text: When reassessing vital signs, compare the baseline set — obtained during the {{c1::primary assessment::assessment phase}} — with any and all subsequent vital signs, and look for trends.
Back Extra:
Cue: the trend questions — have the vitals increased, declined, or stayed the same? If so, how fast?

Why: reassessment exists to identify and treat changes in the patient's condition — also recheck mental status, airway, breathing, circulation, and skin color and temperature.
